hero.title: Lambdas
intro.0: A lambda is a tiny function with no name that you write right where you need it and keep in a variable. This is your first look at them: what they are, how they answer a yes/no question, and the one thing they do that a plain method can't - read the variables sitting around them. Next lesson you'll hand these to LINQ. Write each small program, run it, match the output.
task.1.title: Store it once, call it twice
task.1.context: A lambda is a tiny function with no name. You keep it in a variable and call it as often as you like - that is the point of storing it. `(int legs) => legs + 1` reads: take `legs`, give back `legs + 1`. A stool has three legs, a chair has four; store the 'add a leg' function once and use it on both.
task.1.goal.0: Store a lambda `addLeg` that gives back `legs + 1`.
task.1.goal.1: Call it on `3` and on `4`, printing each result - two lines: `4` then `5`.
task.2.title: Run a rule over a list
task.2.context: A lambda can give back `true` or `false` - a small yes/no test. The useful part is running that one test over many items. Store `isFourLegged` (does a leg count equal four?), then walk the array with a `foreach` and count how many animals pass. This by-hand loop is exactly what LINQ will do for you next lesson.
task.2.goal.0: Store a lambda `isFourLegged` that returns whether a count equals `4`.
task.2.goal.1: Loop over `legs` and count how many pass, then print the count - the output is `2`.
task.3.title: A rule that reads a local
task.3.context: Here is where a lambda earns its keep. Say the threshold sits in a variable, `minLegs`, set a line earlier. A lambda written right there can read `minLegs` on its own - a separate named method could not, it only sees what you pass it. Store `enough` (does a count reach `minLegs`?), then count how many animals clear the bar.
task.3.goal.0: Store a lambda `enough` that returns whether a count is `>= minLegs` (it reads the local `minLegs`).
task.3.goal.1: Loop over `legs` and count how many reach `minLegs`, then print it - the output is `3`.
task.4.title: Configure a step, then run it
task.4.context: Because a lambda can read the values around it, you can bake one in. `bonus` is a plain number; store `reward` so it adds `bonus` to any score. The same lambda now carries `bonus` with it - loop over the scores and print each rewarded total. Change `bonus` once and every result follows.
task.4.goal.0: Store a lambda `reward` that gives back `score + bonus` (it reads the local `bonus`).
task.4.goal.1: Loop over `scores` and print each rewarded total - two lines: `15` then `30`.
task.5.title: Why care about lambdas? - recap
task.5.context: So what is a lambda, and why keep one around?
task.5.summaryIntro: A lambda is a tiny function with no name that you keep in a variable. It is worth caring about because you can package a small rule or step, run it over many items, and - unlike a plain named method - it can read the variables sitting around it.
task.5.summaryItems.0.title: A function in a variable -
task.5.summaryItems.0.text: no name, stored once, called as often as you like.
task.5.summaryItems.1.title: The arrow -
task.5.summaryItems.1.text: `(input) => result`: input on the left, the answer on the right.
task.5.summaryItems.2.title: A rule over a list -
task.5.summaryItems.2.text: one small `foreach` runs your test on every item.
task.5.summaryItems.3.title: Capture -
task.5.summaryItems.3.text: a lambda can read the locals beside it; a named method only sees what you pass it.
task.5.summaryItems.4.title: Configure it -
task.5.summaryItems.4.text: bake in a value you have now, and the same lambda does a new job.
task.5.summaryClose: Next: LINQ - `legs.Count(...)` and `scores.Select(...)` do that same foreach for you, in one line, with a lambda exactly like these. (When a step deserves a real name, a normal method still works - a lambda just wins when it is small, inline, or needs the values around it.)
